[[File:Unusual number Cuisenaire rods 10.png|thumb|Demonstration, with [[Cuisenaire rods]], that the number 10 is an unusual number, its largest prime factor being 5, which is greater than √10 ≈ 3.16]]

In [[number theory]], an '''unusual number''' is a [[natural number]] ''n'' whose largest [[prime factor]] is strictly greater than [[square root|<math>\sqrt{n}</math>]].

A ''k''-[[smooth number]] has all its prime factors less than or equal to ''k'', therefore, an unusual number is non-<math>\sqrt{n}</math>-smooth.

The term "unusual number" was coined by Daniel Greene and [[Donald Knuth]], who also showed that, somewhat confusingly, they are asymptotically more [[Natural density|dense]] than their "usual" counterparts.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Weisstein |first1=Eric |title=Rough Number |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/RoughNumber.html |website=Wolfram MathWorld |access-date=15 April 2026}}</ref>

==Relation to prime numbers==
All [[prime number]]s are unusual.
For any prime ''p'', its multiples less than ''p''<sup>2</sup> are unusual, that is ''p'', ... (''p'' − 1)''p'', which have a density 1/''p'' in the interval (''p'', ''p''<sup>2</sup>).

==Examples==
The first few unusual numbers are
: 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 26, 28, 29, 31, 33, 34, 35, 37, 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 44, 46, 47, 51, 52, 53, 55, 57, 58, 59, 61, 62, 65, 66, 67, ...  {{OEIS|id=A064052}}

The first few non-prime (composite) unusual numbers are
: 6, 10, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22, 26, 28, 33, 34, 35, 38, 39, 42, 44, 46, 51, 52, 55, 57, 58, 62, 65, 66, 68, 69, 74, 76, 77, 78, 82, 85, 86, 87, 88, 91, 92, 93, 94, 95, 99, 102, ... {{OEIS|id=A063763}}

==Distribution==
If we denote the number of unusual numbers less than or equal to ''n'' by ''u''(''n'') then ''u''(''n'') behaves as follows:

[[Richard Schroeppel]] stated in the [[HAKMEM]] (1972), Item #29<ref name="hakmem-29">{{cite journal |author-last=Schroeppel |author-first=Richard |author-link=Richard Schroeppel |editor-first=Henry Givens Jr. |editor-last=Baker |editor-link=Henry Baker (computer scientist) |title=ITEM 29 |journal=[[HAKMEM]] |date=April 1995 |orig-date=1972-02-29 |id=AI Memo 239 Item 29 |publisher=[[MIT AI Lab|Artificial Intelligence Laboratory]], [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA |edition=retyped & converted |url=http://www.inwap.com/pdp10/hbaker/hakmem/number.html#item29 |access-date=2024-06-16 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240224184435/http://www.inwap.com/pdp10/hbaker/hakmem/number.html#item29 |archive-date=2024-02-24}}</ref> that the asymptotic [[probability]] that a randomly chosen number is unusual is [[Natural logarithm of 2|<!-- no italic here!! -->ln(2)]]. In other words:

:<math>\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{u(n)}{n} = \ln(2) = 0.693147 \dots\, .</math>
